newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Moslem states condemn Israel, alarmed over Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Moslem states condemn Israel, alarmed over Bosnia.

text.p: Islamic nations at the end of an annual foreign ministers' meeting on Friday condemned Israeli policies "hostile to peace" and expressed alarm that the Bosnian peace agreement was in jeopardy.
The 54-nation Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC) also gave new impetus to economic cooperation, trade, development and investment during the five-day Jakarta meeting.
But political issues such as Bosnia-Herzegovina and Palestine topped the gathering's agenda.
In one of two declarations issued at the end of the meeting, the ministers said they strongly condemned Israeli policies "which are hostile to peace".
They "expressed their strong denunciation and anger at the threats made by the Israeli officials and which are aimed at taking the region back to a state of war...," the declaration said.

The second declaration said the ministers had "received an alarming message from the highest authorities of the Bosnian people that the spirit and the letter of the Dayton peace agreement have been put in jeopardy".

It appealed to the international community to defend the principles embodied in the Dayton agreement, arrest immediately all indicted war criminals, and "put an end to the manipulation of the destiny of Bosnia and Herzegovina".
The meeting also covered a range of other political issues, including Afghanistan, Somalia and the perennial issue of Indian rule in Jammu and Kashmir.
The OIC decided to leave Kabul's seat vacant during the Jakarta meeting, while urging all warring sides in Afghanistan to form a government of national unity.
Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati told a news conference on Thursday that there was no military solution to the conflict in neighbouring Afghanistan.
Velayati said Afghanistan needed "a broad-based government in which all different ethnic and religious groups should participate" if it was to attain lasting peace.

At the outset of the meeting, host Indonesia pressed for greater focus on economic cooperation among OIC members. Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas told a news conference on Friday the call had been "well received and responded to by every speaker".

He said the OIC had appropriate institutions and mechanisms already in place. What was needed now, he said, was to see why they had not worked in the past, and how to use them effectively in the future.

Former Moroccan Prime Minister Azzadine Laraki was elected unanimously as the sole candidate to the post of OIC secretary-general, replacing Niger's Hamid Algabid, whose eight-year term ends at the end of this month.
The OIC will hold a summit in Tehran in December 1997, while the next meeting of foreign ministers will be in Qatar in March 1998.
